description.narrative: In Uganda, Oxfam Uganda (in coordination with Oxfam Denmark) and the Luigi GiussaniFoundation (LGF), will engage their networks of educators and policymakers to ensure themobilisation of their knowledge. In West Nile, the local government Education TechnicalCommittees, including District Education Officer, District Inspector of Schools and ChiefAdministrative Officer will be involved just as the Uganda National Institute for TeacherEducation (UNITE) and the Commission for Teacher Training at the Ministryof Education. Inline with Oxfam’s Feminist Principle: ‘Nothing About Us Without Us’ teachers will be providedopportunity to directly be involved. Members of Parliament and local and national educationcoordination groups will be involved.LGF brings valuable expertise in improving teacher well-being and retention in contexts ofprotracted displacement. LGF's initiatives in teacher support, including the ‘ResilientLearners,Teachers and Education Systems in South Sudan and Uganda’ project funded by BRiCE, havedemonstrated the effectiveness of peer-based mentoring, real-time feedback mechanisms,and context-specific professional development. These experiences align directly with theproject’s goal of enhancing teacher well-being and retention through proven, adaptablestrategies in challenging environments.A sub-national and a national event will also beorganised by Oxfam Uganda to disseminate the research findings and identify policy actions.5.4 Regional and International Knowledge MobilisationPage 13 / 24 Research planAt the project start, an online presentation will be organised to mobilise regional and nationalexpertise on EiE, with invitations to the Agence Universitaire de la Francophonie, of which ISPBukavu is a member, the education clusters/working groups of the DRC and Uganda, the RTIA,the Inter-agency Network forEducation in Emergencies (INEE), the Education, Science,Technology and Innovation under the African Union including the Teacher DevelopmentCluster and CIEFFA, UNESCO’s International Institutefor Capacity Building in Africa (IICBA)and other regional entities engaged with teachers and teacher education.At the end, Oxfam Uganda will organise a regional learning event in Kampala, bringing togethernational and regional education stakeholders, policy makers, and researchers. The researchwill also be presented at dedicated IDS and Sussex School of Education seminar, as well asthe annual conferences of the Comparative and International Education Society and the BritishAssociation for International and Comparative Education. The findings will be shared with theINEE through the Teachers in Crisis Context working group (TiCC), of which Oxfam is amember.An open access dissemination plan, in line with FAIR principles of open science, will ensurethat theproject’s academic and policy outputs are available open access on the IDS website,and shared throughthe social media channels of IDS, ISP Bukavu, LGF and Oxfam.6. RESEARCH ETHICS AND RESPONSIBLE SCIENCEThe project will undergo three ethics reviews; first, IDS’s Research Ethics Committee will followthe IDS Research Ethics Policy and undertake a robust process which involves reviews bysenior research staff and the IDS Director of Research. Second, a national ethics review willbe undertaken bythe Comité National D’Ethique de la Santé of the DRC Health ministry, whichhas authority to review all research projects in the DRC. The third will be undertaken by theMildmay Uganda Research <(>&<)> Ethics Committee (MUREC). The project will also ensurecompliance with the Finnish National Agency and European Union guidelines on researchethics. Key ethical issues are:6.1 Physical Safety and Security of Researchers and ParticipantsThe research will be conducted in crisis-affected contexts of the DRC and Uganda. To mitigaterisks to researchers’ and respondent’s safety, a detailed security protocol will be developed. Itwill include security assessments carried out with local authorities, a categorisation of risklevels and a replacement strategy in case specific sites are deemed too risky for fieldwork. Allresearchers will travel with necessary authorisations, communicate their movements daily withproject supervisors, follow curfew hours for travel, and, whenever necessary to stay overnight,only be authorised to do so in towns and accommodation that demonstrably ensure a low tomoderate level of security risk.Measures will be taken to ensure the safety and security of all participants. The study will bepresented to school communities in public meetings to encourage trust-building andtransparency. Appropriate notice will be given to participants, and we will ensure no participantfeels pressured to participate. Informed consent will be sought from participants, including viaa presentation on the research protocols done in advance of the study in order to discuss andassess risks to participants prior to implementation of the research. If any risk is identified fora study site or participant, the study will be temporarily or permanently suspended and areplacement strategy applied.6.2 Conducting Research on Hardship, Violenceand TraumaPage 14 / 24 Research planConducting research on hardship, violence and trauma raises serious ethical issues, which theresearch team has significant experience in navigating. All research and knowledgemobilisation activities will be conducted using trauma- and resilience-informed researchprinciples and practice (Edelman 2023), which were developed by a trauma specialist andadapted to the eastern DRC context during a previous project (Marchais et al. 2022). Theseensure that participants feel safe during interviews, have advance notice of the questionnairesbefore being asked for their informed consent, ensure that any sign of unease during theinterview is detected and acted upon, and are offered followupsupport. Research andknowledge mobilisation instruments will be developed in a modulable way, to allow sections ofthe questionnaires/focus group interviews related to hardship, violence and trauma to beremoved for certain participants, who will be categorised as: a) Expert/academic/policymaker;b) teacher trainer/headteacher/teacher/school staff; or c) parent/community member. Only thefirst two categories will be given sections related to hardship, violence and trauma, in order toreduce the inherent risk of triggering traumatic memories among vulnerable participants whendiscussing difficult experiences (Corbellini 2023). A second informed-consent sheet willprecede sensitive sections of the questionnaires, presenting the questions and reiterating thatparticipants are free to skip them, along with a rapid assessment of the participant’s level ofvulnerability. If participants express reserves about answering questions or present signs ofdistress, these sections will be skipped.6.3 Ethical Research PartnershipsThe research team has reflected and written about equitable partnerships (Marchais et al.2020; Wandji et al. 2022), and the project will work to actively counter the knowledge, materialand professional hierarchies that exist in such research configurations, adopting a criticallyreflexive approach to the partnership (Shah et al. 2023). The project and consortium will alsobuild on the Pathways to impactful and equitable partnerships in Research for Development,led by Southern Voices and IDS.6.4 Responsible ScienceIDS will coordinate with partners to ensure that the EU’s Open Science principles are respectedthroughout the project; all project outputs will open and free to access, datasets will beanonymised and published through an online data repository, andstakeholders’ and end users’knowledge will be engaged throughout the process.7. SOCIETAL EFFECTS AND IMPACT7.1 Policy ImpactThe research holds significant potential to influence education policy in the DRC and Uganda.In the DRC, our research focus aligns with theEducation Sector Strategy 2016-25, whichemphasises reforming teacher recruitment systems, and the 2022 Partnership Compact, whichisaimed at revitalising the teaching profession for a more resilient education sector(Government of the DRC 2015,2022). Our work willoffer evidence-based recommendationsfor policy improvements. It will directly be inputted into these policies by SPACE, and alsoinform the new education sector strategy, which SPACE is currently developing.In Uganda, the EducationandSports Sector Strategic Plan (ESSP), the Partnership Compactand the National Teacher Policy underscore the need for professional development andeffective teacher management in response to population growth and refugee influxes (MES2019, 2020, 2022). Our project will provide insights on teachermanagement reforms, such asthe impact of salary incentives for teachers in remote areas and the effectiveness of thePage 15 / 24 Research planTeacher Management and Information System (Arinaitwe et al. 2020). Additionally, theEducation Response Plan for Refugees and Host Communities emphasises teacher peer-based professional support as critical to addressing overcrowded classrooms and improvinglearning outcomes (MES 2018), although earlier efforts have faced challenges likeunderfunding and coordination gaps (Oxfam 2021), and additional difficulties are appearing asa result of the profound changes that the education sector is undergoing as a result of theTeacher Bill reform.The research will also have a broader regional impact, aligning with the African Union’sContinental EducationStrategy for Africa 2016-2025 (CESA) and initiatives by organisationslike the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). Byaddressing teacher well-being and retention, the project contributes to building resilient education systems acrossAfrica, aligningwith Agenda 2063 and the Kampala Convention on Internal Displacement,which advocate for educational access as a crisis response priority.7.2 Use of Research by Relevant StakeholdersThe research findings will be highly relevant for education ministries and schooladministrations in the DRC and Uganda, who will leverage the results to refine policiespromoting teacher well-being and retention, integrating strategies into frameworks like theDRC’s education sector plan and Uganda’s Education Response Plan (Brandt 2019; Kjær <(>&<)>Muwanga 2019). School administrations can use the findings to improve teacher management,ensuring more equitable deployment and enhancing support structures inconflict-affectedareas, building on existing successful practices which will have been identified by the project.The findings will also be relevant for teacher training institutions aiming to develop crisis-responsive training modules, focusing on managing trauma and integrating psychosocialsupport (Education Cannot Wait 2022). ISP Bukavu is currently developing a pre-serviceteacher training module on the topic, to be incorporated into the national curriculum of teachertraining institutes in the DRC, andthe results will directly inform the development of the moduleand impact generations of teachers deployed to crisis affected contexts. It will also be of useto education researchers, who will be reached through the National Doctoral School oneducation,which is based at ISP Bukavu and directed by Professor Mashanda, who is part ofthe research team.Education organisations and NGO, including LGF and Oxfam, will also use the results toimplement successful peer collaboration models identified in the research, reinforcing teachernetworks, wellbeing and instructional quality (Mendenhall et al. 2025; UNESCO <(>&<)> InternationalTask Force on Teachers for Education 2030, 2024). Oxfam Uganda’s and Oxfam in Africa’srobust networks and ongoing educational programmes across Africa provide an ideal platformto amplifying the project’s impact on a regional scale.This comprehensive approach ensures that the projectnot only addresses immediateeducational challenges but also lays the groundwork for systemic improvements in teacherretention and well-being, with wider societal benefits.7.3 Societal ImpactThis project will contribute to more resilient and equitable education systems in crisis-affectedregions. In the short term, the project’s capacity-building efforts are expectedto empowerteachers and administrators in regions like Beni in the DRC and West Nile in Uganda. Byinforming teacher support programs, the project seeks to fosterprofessional communities,enhance school environments, and address immediate needs. In the medium term, wePage 16 / 24 Research plananticipate increased teacher retention, which will contribute to the stability of educationsystems and ensure consistent, high-quality learning experiences for students in crisiscontexts (Mendenhall et al. 2024; Falk et al. 2022). This continuity is crucial for academicachievement and socio-emotional development, as sustained teacher-student relationshipsare linked to higher student performance and well-being (Shephard et al. 2024). Long-termbenefits may include stronger school cultures, reduced class size disruptions, andmoreresilient communities (Wolf et al. 2015; UNESCO 2024).By highlighting the unique challenges that refugee teachers face—such as emotional strain,language barriers, resource scarcity, and the needto bridge cultural divides—the study willalso raise awareness andstrengthen advocacy for targeted support for these teachers,including with regards to mental health and well-being. Through stronger policy, institutionaland societal support, teachers in crisis-affected and refugee settings will experience improvedjob satisfaction and mental health, benefiting the education system as a whole.The results of the study will also benefit crisis-affected and refugee communities by raisingeducational standards.Refugee learners, who frequently depend on education for stability anddevelopment, benefit from teachers who feel supported because they are better able to provideconsistent and effective instruction. Furthermore, aseducators serve as community leaders,enhancingtheir wellbeing may promote harmony and goodwill between the host and refugeepopulations, facilitating social integration.Beyond Uganda and the DRC, the study's findings may stimulate comparable studies andinitiativeselsewhere, especially in East, Central and West Africa and in countries impacted bycrises. The study can promote well-being activities in contexts of vulnerability and break thestigma associated with mental health disorders in African societies. The study's focusonteacher well-being may serve as a template for enhancing educational systems in times ofcrisis around the world, ultimately advancing educational equity and resilience.8. REFERENCESACLED (2023) 'ACLED Year in Review: Global Disorder in 2022', Armed Conflict Location andEvent Data.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam Novib is one of the 17 national affiliates of the Oxfam International Confederation. It started life in 1956 as the Netherlands Organisation for International Assistance (Novib), and joined forces with Oxfam in 1994. Working together in confederation, the Oxfam affiliates can speak with one clear and compelling voice on issues of global concern: climate change, health and education forall, agriculture, trade, and conflicts and emergencies. Oxfam established this country office to support local organizations and projects. Through this local office Oxfam Novib directly contributes towards this project’s implementation.
